question.name: Question 2
question.problem: For the function $f(x,y,z)=x{y}^{2}-2yz+z$, find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,-1,1).$
question.worked_solution:
A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,-1,1)$ can be found by computing 
$∇f(1,-1,1).$ 

So, we first find the gradient of $f(x,y,z)$  and evaluate it at $(x,y,z)=(1,-1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{y}^{2}-2yz+z)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(x{y}^{2}-2yz+z)\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(x{y}^{2}-2yz+z)\,k \\  & ={y}^{2}\text{ }i+(2xy-2z)\text{ }j+(-2y+1)\text{ }k \\ ∇f(1,-1,1) & =(-1)^{2}\,i+(2(1)(-1)-2(1))\,j+(-2(-1)+1)\,k \\  & =1\,i-4j+3\,k\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, $\,i-4\,j+3\,k$ is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,-1,1).$
